briefing.opening: Hello everyone. We will now begin the climate briefing for October 1, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Global Climate Emergency: Unprecedented Impacts on Ecosystems and Society
sections.content: Severe impacts of climate change are being reported globally. Glaciers in the Swiss Alps have shrunk by 5.5% this year alone, with approximately 20% lost over the past five years, indicating a 'catastrophic' level of ice loss that threatens water supplies [4, 13, 174, 176]. In Greece, disappearing lakes reveal the rapid effects of climate change [144, 167], and despite adapting to floods, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam faces increasing threats due to climate change [145, 159, 171, 173]. Furthermore, devastating wildfires caused by El Niño have occurred in Indonesian orangutan habitats, causing immense damage and realizing severe threats to biodiversity [180]. Climate change is also significantly affecting global skin health, exacerbating specific skin conditions, and contributing to rising food prices, thereby increasing economic burdens [153, 155, 160, 168].

sections.title: ⚠️ Changing Landscapes: Agricultural Adaptation and Policy Challenges
sections.content: Climate change is bringing unpredictable shifts. The news that rice farming has occurred for the first time in Dutch wetlands, previously used for cattle grazing, is being hailed as an 'unexpected harvest unimaginable 20 years ago,' signaling rapid changes in agricultural environments [1, 3, 6]. However, recognizing and responding to these changes still presents challenges. Proposed science standards in Florida, USA, include content that downplays evolution and climate change, once again highlighting the importance of climate education [150, 152]. Meanwhile, domestically, 9 out of 10 seniors aged 60 and above perceive climate change as a serious threat, demonstrating a high level of public awareness [5].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 South Korea's Carbon Neutrality Drive: The Gap Between Goals and Reality
sections.content: Various local governments in South Korea are making active efforts to achieve carbon neutrality. Chungju City has declared its vision to become a 'leading carbon-neutral city,' aiming for a 43.9% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and net-zero by 2050 [21, 25, 28, 29, 30, 55, 57, 67, 74, 78, 83]. Naju City has also achieved tangible results, being selected as an excellent local government in carbon neutrality implementation for two consecutive years [35, 47, 48, 58, 73]. Efforts to promote daily practices, such as Gwangmyeong City's 'Citizen Climate Tour' to encourage citizen participation [42, 77], and Gimpo City and Boryeong City's operation of carbon neutrality point systems [31, 56, 65, 80], are also ongoing. Nevertheless, basic local governments in Gyeongsangnam-do and the Daegu-Gyeongbuk regions have shown that many challenges remain, failing to meet greenhouse gas reduction targets in the building and transportation sectors [32, 34, 39, 45].

sections.title: 🌱 Accelerating Renewable Energy Transition: Policy Commitment and Infrastructure Expansion
sections.content: Minister Kim Sung-hwan of the Ministry of Climate stated that renewable energy will be expanded by over 10 GW annually starting next year, assessing South Korea's renewable energy transition as being in the 'take-off phase' [86, 88, 92, 97, 98, 107, 109, 116, 118, 120, 121, 125, 126]. The government announced plans to increase transmission grid capacity by 52 GW to meet the 2030 target of 100 GW of renewable energy, demonstrating its commitment to infrastructure expansion [102, 105]. Furthermore, community energy models, such as 'resident-led energy transition' which returns solar power generation profits to villages, are being emphasized as key to securing economic viability and creating jobs, and are thus expanding [85, 93, 95, 99, 100, 114, 130]. However, numerous policy and infrastructure-related challenges remain, including controversy over the reform of the Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS) [108], issues with grid connection for offshore wind power in the Incheon area [134], and the potential for 1.2 to 1.3 trillion KRW in penalties for the Korea Rural Community Corporation if it fails to meet its renewable energy obligations [84, 135].

briefing.closing: In today's briefing, we examined the severe global impacts of climate change, along with various domestic and international response efforts and the challenges encountered in that process. Sustained attention and cooperation are crucial for addressing the climate crisis. This concludes today's climate briefing.
